title: Feature Scaling I - Standardization
abstract:
Standardization — also called Z-score normalization — rescales a column to
mean $0$ and standard deviation $1$ using $x' = (x-\bar{x})/\sigma$. This
document covers why scaling is needed at all (the distance-domination problem),
the formula and what each symbol means, exactly which algorithms break without
it and which are completely indifferent, the geometry of what standardization
does and does not change, measured evidence of the effect, and the fit-on-train
rule that makes it correct.

blocks.t: Why Scaling Exists
From the notes

Feature scaling is a technique to standardize the independent features
present in the data in a fixed range. We use it to prevent a feature
from dominating. It is generally the last thing we do in the feature
engineering pipeline, right before feeding the data to the model.
The domination problem, worked

The notes give the example directly. Suppose age is in the range of
$100$s and salary is in the range of $10{,}000$s. KNN computes Euclidean
distance:
Take two customers:

The age difference of 30 years contributes $900$ out of $1{,}000{,}900$ —
$0.09\%$ of the distance. The salary term dominates completely. A
30-year age gap is effectively invisible to the algorithm, not because age is
unimportant but because it is measured in smaller units.
The unit-arbitrariness argument

Change salary from rupees to lakhs and the model's predictions change completely.
But nothing about the world changed — only your choice of unit. Any algorithm
whose answer depends on your choice of units is broken, and scaling is what
removes that dependence.
The Formula
Standardization / Z-score normalization
\boxed{ x_i' = \frac{x_i-\bar{x}}{\sigma} }

rows: the standard deviation of the column

blocks.t:
The result has $\textbf{mean}=0$ and $\textbf{std}=1$. That is the range of the
scaled column.
Proof that the mean becomes 0 and the std becomes 1

\operatorname{Var}(x')=\operatorname{Var} \left(\frac{x-\bar x}{\sigma}\right)
 =\frac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\operatorname{Var}(x)=\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\sigma^{2}}=1 .

Two facts follow, and both are used constantly: subtracting a constant does not
change the variance, and dividing by a constant $c$ divides the variance by
$c^2$.
What standard deviation actually tells you

The notes flag this explicitly. Standard deviation tells you the spread
of the data from the average:

items: Small $\sigma$ $\Rightarrow$ values are close to the mean.
Large $\sigma$ $\Rightarrow$ values are spread far apart.

blocks.t:
So dividing by $\sigma$ is asking: how many typical spreads away from
average is this value? A $z$ of $+2$ means the same thing for age as for salary
— "unusually high" — and that common meaning is exactly what makes the
features comparable.
What Standardization Changes and What It Does Not

blocks.cap:
Standardisation centres the cloud at the origin and
 rescales each axis. It does not rotate, and — as the right panel shows
 — it does not change the shape of the distribution.

blocks.t: Standardization does not make data normal

This is the most common misconception about it. $x'=(x-\bar x)/\sigma$ is a
linear map — it shifts and stretches, nothing more. A right-skewed
column is exactly as skewed after standardisation as before. If you want to
change the shape, you need a non-linear transform: log, square-root,
Box-Cox or Yeo-Johnson (Topics 18–19). "Z-score normalization" is an
unfortunate name that has misled a generation.
Which Algorithms Need It

blocks.cap:
Three tiers. Distance- and variance-based methods are broken without
 scaling. Gradient-based methods still converge but far more slowly. Tree-based
 methods are entirely indifferent.

blocks.t: Broken without it — distance and variance based

KNN, K-Means, SVM with an RBF kernel, and PCA. All of them combine features into
a single scalar — a distance or a variance — so the feature with the largest
numeric range dominates that scalar, as computed in \S1.1. PCA is the starkest
case: it maximises variance, and variance is measured in the square of whatever
unit you happened to choose.
Affected — gradient based
Why gradient descent slows down without scaling

For linear regression with squared loss, the Hessian is $H=\frac{2}{n}X^{\!\top}X$.
Gradient descent converges at a rate governed by the condition number
\kappa(H)=\frac{\lambda_{\max}}{\lambda_{\min}},

the ratio of the largest to smallest eigenvalue. If one feature ranges over
$[0,1]$ and another over $[0,10^5]$, then $\kappa$ is on the order of $10^{10}$:
the loss surface is a long, thin valley, and gradient descent zig-zags across it
instead of running down it. The number of iterations needed scales roughly with
$\sqrt{\kappa}$.

Standardising every feature to unit variance makes the diagonal of $X^{\!\top}X$
uniform, collapsing $\kappa$ towards 1 and turning the valley into a bowl.

The notes make exactly this point: standardisation is used in gradient
based algorithms — linear regression, logistic regression, SVM, and all of
deep learning.
Indifferent — tree based
Why trees do not care

The notes state it plainly: not tree based — decision trees, random
forests, XGBoost. A tree asks "is salary $\le 47{,}500$?". It considers
one feature at a time and only uses the ordering of that feature's values.
Any strictly increasing transform — including standardisation — leaves the
ordering unchanged, therefore leaves every split unchanged, therefore leaves the
tree identical. Scaling a tree's inputs is not wrong; it is simply a no-op.
Measured

blocks.cap:
A dataset in which the truth depends only on age, with salary
 present as a large-magnitude irrelevant feature. KNN collapses to near-chance
 without scaling and recovers completely with it.

blocks.t: Fit on Train, Apply to Test

blocks.cap:
The rule the notes repeat throughout: you fit on TRAIN data and
 apply on TEST data. The scaler learns $\bar x$ and $\sigma$ once, from
 training data, and reuses them everywhere else.

blocks.t: Two ways to get this wrong

1. Fitting on the whole dataset.
StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_all) before splitting leaks the test
distribution into the training statistics. Metrics become optimistic.

2. Fitting separately on test.
scaler.fit_transform(X_test) is worse. Train and test are now on
different scales — the same raw salary maps to different numbers in the
two sets — and the model receives inputs it has never seen the units of.

Correct: fit_transform on train, transform on test. The test set's
scaled mean will not be exactly 0, and that is precisely right — it
reflects genuine distributional difference rather than being forced away.
Code

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression, SGDClassifier
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 4000
age    = rng.uniform(20, 60, n)
salary = rng.uniform(20_000, 150_000, n)
X = np.c_[age, salary]
y = (age > 40).astype(int)             # THE TRUTH DEPENDS ONLY ON AGE

X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.25, random_state=0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. THE DOMINATION PROBLEM, MEASURED
# =====================================================================
a, b = np.array([25, 50_000]), np.array([55, 51_000])
diff2 = (b - a) ** 2
print("squared differences:", diff2)              # [    900 1000000]
print("distance:", np.sqrt(diff2.sum()).round(2)) # 1000.45
print("age contributes", f"{diff2[0] / diff2.sum():.4%}")   # 0.0899%

# =====================================================================
# 2. STANDARDIZATION -- fit on TRAIN only
# =====================================================================
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_tr_s = scaler.fit_transform(X_tr)    # LEARNS mean and std here
X_te_s = scaler.transform(X_te)        # REUSES them -- does NOT relearn

print("learned mean :", scaler.mean_.round(1))     # from TRAIN
print("learned scale:", scaler.scale_.round(1))    # sqrt of learned variance
print("train scaled mean:", X_tr_s.mean(axis=0).round(6))  # exactly ~0
print("train scaled std :", X_tr_s.std(axis=0).round(6))   # exactly ~1
print("test  scaled mean:", X_te_s.mean(axis=0).round(4))  # NOT 0 -- correct!

# =====================================================================
# 3. FROM SCRATCH -- there is nothing hidden in it
# =====================================================================
mu    = X_tr.mean(axis=0)
sigma = X_tr.std(axis=0)               # note: numpy ddof=0, same as sklearn
manual_tr = (X_tr - mu) / sigma
manual_te = (X_te - mu) / sigma        # <-- the SAME mu and sigma
print("matches sklearn:", np.allclose(manual_tr, X_tr_s),
                          np.allclose(manual_te, X_te_s))

# =====================================================================
# 4. WHO ACTUALLY CARES
# =====================================================================
models = {
    "KNN (distance)":        KNeighborsClassifier(5),
    "Logistic (gradient)":   LogisticRegression(max_iter=200),
    "Decision Tree (splits)": DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4, random_state=0),
}
print(f"{'model':24s} {'raw':>8s} {'scaled':>8s}")
for name, m in models.items():
    raw = cross_val_score(m, X, y, cv=5).mean()
    sc  = cross_val_score(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), m), X, y, cv=5).mean()
    print(f"{name:24s} {raw:8.3f} {sc:8.3f}")
# KNN:    ~0.55 -> ~0.97   (broken -> fixed)
# LogReg: ~0.78 -> ~0.99   (converges properly)
# Tree:   ~0.99 -> ~0.99   (identical -- scaling is a NO-OP for trees)

# Proof that a tree is literally unchanged:
t1 = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4, random_state=0).fit(X_tr, y_tr)
t2 = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4, random_state=0).fit(X_tr_s, y_tr)
print("identical predictions:",
      (t1.predict(X_te) == t2.predict(X_te_s)).all())     # True

# =====================================================================
# 5. CONVERGENCE SPEED -- the condition-number effect
# =====================================================================
H_raw = X_tr.T @ X_tr / len(X_tr)
H_scl = X_tr_s.T @ X_tr_s / len(X_tr_s)
cond = lambda H: np.linalg.cond(H)
print(f"condition number  raw {cond(H_raw):.3e}   scaled {cond(H_scl):.3f}")

for tag, data in [("raw", X_tr), ("scaled", X_tr_s)]:
    sgd = SGDClassifier(loss="log_loss", max_iter=2000, tol=1e-4,
                        random_state=0).fit(data, y_tr)
    print(f"{tag:7s} epochs to converge: {sgd.n_iter_}")

# =====================================================================
# 6. STANDARDIZATION DOES NOT MAKE DATA NORMAL
# =====================================================================
from scipy import stats
skewed = rng.lognormal(3, .9, 5000)
z = StandardScaler().fit_transform(skewed.reshape(-1, 1)).ravel()
print(f"skew before {stats.skew(skewed):.3f}  after {stats.skew(z):.3f}")  # SAME
print(f"log-transform skew: {stats.skew(np.log(skewed)):.3f}")  # THIS reshapes
# Standardization is LINEAR. To change the shape you need Topics 18-19.

# =====================================================================
# 7. THE CORRECT WAY: put it in a Pipeline so it cannot leak
# =====================================================================
pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(5))
pipe.fit(X_tr, y_tr)                   # scaler fitted on train folds only
print("test accuracy:", pipe.score(X_te, y_te))
# Inside cross_val_score, the scaler is refitted on each training fold --
# doing it by hand outside the CV loop leaks across folds.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
Feature scaling standardises the independent features into a fixed
 range, to prevent a feature from dominating. It is the
 last step of the feature-engineering pipeline.

Standard deviation measures spread from the average: small $\sigma$
 means values cluster near the mean; large $\sigma$ means they are spread
 far apart.

Used in gradient-based algorithms (linear, logistic, SVM, deep
 learning) — not tree based.

Mandatory for distance/variance methods: KNN, K-Means, SVM-RBF,
 PCA. Helpful for gradient methods (condition number $\to$ faster
 convergence). Irrelevant for trees, which use only rank order.

It centres and rescales; it does not change the shape of the
 distribution and does not make data normal.

Fit on TRAIN, apply on TEST. The test set's scaled mean will not
 be exactly zero — that is correct.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Does standardisation make data normally distributed?

No. It is a linear transform — it shifts and stretches. Skewness and kurtosis
are unchanged. To alter the shape you need a non-linear transform such as log or
Box-Cox.
Q. Why don't decision trees need scaling?

A tree splits on one feature at a time using a threshold, so it depends only on
the ordering of values within a feature. Standardisation is monotonic, so
the ordering — and therefore every split and the entire tree — is unchanged.
Q. You standardised the test set separately and results got worse. Why?

Train and test are now on different scales: the same raw value maps to different
numbers in each set. The model was fitted in the training set's coordinate
system and is being asked to predict in a different one. Fit once on train,
transform both.
Q. Why does scaling speed up gradient descent?

It lowers the condition number of the Hessian. Unscaled features produce a long,
narrow loss valley in which gradient descent zig-zags; iterations needed scale
roughly with $\sqrt{\kappa}$. Unit variance across features makes the valley
closer to circular.
Q. Should you scale the target variable in regression?

Usually not necessary, but it can help with gradient stability when the target is
very large. If you do, remember to invert the transform before reporting metrics
— an RMSE in standardised units is meaningless to a stakeholder. Use
TransformedTargetRegressor so the inversion is automatic.
Q. Standardisation or normalisation — which do you pick?

Standardisation when the data is roughly Gaussian, when outliers are present,
and for gradient-based models. Min-Max normalisation when the data has known
fixed bounds — image pixels in $[0,255]$ — and for distance-based models.
That is Topic 14.
